doc.title: Roger Kellaway interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

title: Technology, Sibelius and early electronic music
summary: He writes with pencil and paper, uses midi as a tool, and recalls Stockhausen and Alwin Nikolais.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I was just going to — yeah, you made me think of — does your curiosity extend into the available technology these days to supposedly make your life more creative?
It doesn’t make it more creative. And it doesn’t make it faster.
You can see where I’m coming from too.

Those are the two things. I went to the NAMM show a couple of years ago, and I went up to get a demonstration of Sibelius software, which I’d been interested in, it’s a writing program. This guy proceeded to show me how to compose with the computer. As I was watching this I kept saying to him no, no, no, no, no. I’m not interested in this. I will never be interested in this. And he said, “Let me show you how to do this.” And I kept saying my line and he kept — this is what he was going to show me because he’s programmed to show me. I said, “Look, let me get this idea straight to you. I write with a pencil and paper. That is how I write. I am an acoustic person. It has to do with the emotion that my body feels from the ideas going on the paper, and the pencil of it is the hands of the earth or however you want to think of it metaphorically. And I will use the midi and computer to realize that. I haven’t quite got all this through my head yet even, that I don’t need to ever go to the studio in a way to do something that’s 80 or 90 pieces, when I have all of the samples available to me, I’m learning how to hard drive and record and all of those things. But the main ideas go down on paper. I couldn’t possibly spend my time clicking a mouse for one note. When you go [whistles] and you’ve got a whole chord. And you can assign it to 40 people in a second. No, no, no, no. That’s nonsense. But the idea of perhaps playing an idea into a synthesizer and suddenly having it printed out for you, that’s great. I think that’s a boon. And we need to have, I think, combinations of synthetic music and acoustic music, it’s going to be okay. I do find it ironic however when people talk about so-called electronic music because when I think of electronic music I think of Stockhausen and Dofschtetter and Luening and Ussachevsky and all the people from the 60s that I used to listen to that didn’t have any of these instruments. Edgar Varese and they were just doing tape manipulation and it was so adventurous and imaginative. Alwin Nicoli, did you ever—
No I’m not familiar with him.

Alwin Nicoli what a guy. I was hanging out with some kind of out people in New York that really loved avante garde. Once they discovered that I did they took me down to hear Alwin Nicoli one night. And Alwin Nicoli Dance Company, he did the costumes, the lighting, the choreography and the music. And what was astounding, I can remember one piece that he did where he had this whole huge piece of plexiglass that came down behind the dancers and the dancers had wrist bands that were attacked to the plexiglas so that © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-
every time they made a movement they stretched the plexiglas into a different shape and lights would cascade around — what is this? Yeah it was crazy.
